The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But this immediately raised another question: how should the caliph be chosen?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Should he be appointed or elected?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Who had the right to make the appointment?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
And who had the right to take part in the election?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In practice, events themselves answered these questions before any clear theory had been settled.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The meeting at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida, which ended with Abū Bakr becoming caliph after a personal initiative by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, became the first historical model for deciding how a caliph might be chosen.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Then Abū Bakr personally selected ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to succeed him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar later used a different method, which became known as shūrā, or consultation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

After he received the wound that eventually killed him, he was asked to appoint a successor. Instead, he chose six men from among the Companions and instructed them to meet for three days after his death and select one of themselves as caliph.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He laid down the procedure in considerable detail.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Indeed, the arrangement was so carefully directed that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who was one of the six, seems to have expected the outcome from the moment he left ʿUmar’s meeting after the plan was announced.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He told a group of Banū Hāshim who were with him:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“If your people have their way, none of you will ever be given power.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“It has been turned away from us...”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf carried out the plan that ʿUmar had drawn up before his death, and the members of the shūrā eventually chose ʿUthmān as the third caliph after ʿUmar.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
After ʿUthmān was killed during the well-known uprising against him, the process became much more spontaneous.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At that point, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the obvious candidate. Some people pledged allegiance to him, others fought him, and still others remained neutral, as we will see.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
A great deal has been written about the principle of shūrā in Islamic literature. The period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs has even been called the “age of shūrā.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But what exactly does this principle mean?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Some modern Muslim scholars define shūrā as consultation among Muslims in choosing the caliph and in dealing with public affairs and the government of the Islamic state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Did the way the Rightly Guided Caliphs were actually chosen match this definition?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The historical picture we have just described answers the question.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It shows what actually happened, step by step, from the caliphate of Abū Bakr to that of ʿAlī.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Can we really see in these events a practical application of shūrā in the sense described by many modern Islamic writers?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
On the basis of this historical example, the answer seems clear.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The principle of shūrā was not actually applied as a general rule in the government of the Islamic state. In practice, the system took other forms that did not match the meaning that Muslim scholars later gave to the term—even during the reign of ʿUmar, which is often regarded as the golden age of the Rightly Guided Caliphate.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That is the general picture when we look at how shūrā worked in practice.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Now let us look at its legal status.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The primary Islamic texts—the Qur’an and the Sunna—do not contain any clear statement making shūrā a binding principle of law. In other words, it is not explicitly presented as part of Islamic law in the same way as other rules that Muslims are required to follow.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The clearest Qur’anic text on the subject says:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Their affairs are conducted through consultation among themselves.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the verse does not present consultation as a legal rule. It appears as part of a description of the moral qualities and conduct of believers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Nor does the verse say that it applies specifically to government.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If it did clearly lay down a system of political rule, it would be difficult to explain why the Rightly Guided Caliphs were chosen in the ways we have just described.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Some of those choices were shaped by family, tribal, and group interests, if not by interests with something close to a class character.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Others were shaped by personal positions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Still others involved a kind of shūrā from above, in which the people allowed to take part were limited to a small number of individuals.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

And it was already known that these men were unlikely to agree on the person most qualified to become caliph. They had political conflicts among themselves. Each had his own ambition for the office. And most of them had already agreed, in practice, to keep ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib away from leadership of the caliphal state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The principle of shūrā that can be drawn from the Qur’anic verse is therefore broad and unrestricted. It is not defined in enough detail to serve as a binding legal rule that determines the specific form of government in Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muslim scholars themselves acknowledge that Islam did not specify a particular method for carrying out shūrā.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It can still be said, however, that the general spirit of Islamic law rules out the hereditary system that Muʿāwiya later adopted.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One piece of evidence is a saying attributed to the Prophet in which he rejects a system he calls mulkan ʿaḍūḍan—literally, a kingship that “bites” or clings tightly.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The expression is figurative. It can mean a ruler who grips power tightly and keeps its privileges for himself and his heirs. It can also mean a ruler who forces his rule upon the community and holds it there by force. This is how one modern scholar explains the phrase.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But even this prophetic saying is not enough to give the principle of shūrā a clearly defined legal status.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The only other possible basis would be actual practice: the conduct of the Prophet and of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Prophet often consulted his Companions on matters for which no revealed text had given a direct ruling.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Before deciding to fight the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, for example, he consulted them at length until he received their agreement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Similar examples can be found in the conduct of all the Rightly Guided Caliphs except ʿUthmān.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But these examples generally concern legal, administrative, or military matters. They do not establish shūrā as a binding principle covering the entire system of government.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can therefore conclude that Islam does not prescribe one particular form of government that Muslims must follow and no other.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In the end, shūrā is best understood as a recommended principle. Islam encourages Muslims to use it when the public interest requires it.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In other words, the public interest is what should ultimately guide the choice of a system of government.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

1 — Islamic Policy in the Arabian Peninsula
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During the first years after the Hijra, much of Islamic law and policy was directed toward the immediate tasks facing the new movement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The first goal was to bring all the regions of the Arabian Peninsula under one authority and unite them within a system that went beyond the tribal order, which had already exhausted its historical role.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Islam aimed to establish a social order at a higher stage of human development and to turn Mecca and the Kaʿba into an Islamic center that would attract the Arabs of the entire peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
When the Prophet died, this policy had not yet fully achieved its aims.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The people of Mecca and Medina were by then fully under Islamic authority, as were some of the tribes living nearby.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the population of other parts of the peninsula—especially Yemen, Ḥaḍramawt, and Oman in the south—had not yet submitted completely to the Islamic movement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Ridda Wars revealed this historical reality, despite the way Arab historians of the ninth and tenth centuries later described the situation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

It is true that during the “Year of Delegations,” after the Muslims had defeated the leaders of Quraysh and returned to Mecca as conquerors, delegations came to the Prophet from different parts of the peninsula. They announced either their acceptance of Islam or their submission to the authority of the new religion.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But this appearance did not tell the whole story.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Even tribes such as Asad and Ghaṭafān, which lived near Medina—the Islamic capital after the Hijra and the first center of Muslim power—took advantage of the revolt in other regions and joined it themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They were also encouraged by the military situation at the time, because the main core of the Islamic army was outside the peninsula fighting the Romans.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The revolt stretched from Bahrain and Oman along the coast of the Arabian Gulf in the east and southeast, then through Ḥaḍramawt and Yemen in the south, and from there to al-Yamāma.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It therefore formed something close to a semicircle around a large part of the Arabian Peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These conflicts became known as the “Ridda Wars,” or wars of apostasy.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the word ridda covered more than one kind of break with Islamic authority.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Some tribes were refusing obedience to the new tax system, especially the payment of zakāt.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Other tribes, particularly in al-Yamāma, rejected Islam itself.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Taken as a whole, these wars could be described in modern language as wars of counterrevolution.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Their main social character was reactionary because, in their general direction, they stood against the progressive side of the Islamic movement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
2 — The Social Causes of the Ridda Wars
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Ridda Wars represented the social side of the reaction that immediately followed the Prophet’s death.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It would therefore be wrong to explain them simply as a religious return from Islam. That would be a one-sided and idealist explanation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Social factors also lay behind the movement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We have already discussed the growing differences in wealth inside the tribes.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At one end were poor tribespeople who owned almost nothing—not even livestock in many Bedouin areas.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the other end were tribal chiefs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Besides holding money earned through services provided to trading caravans, these chiefs possessed expensive household goods associated with a more settled way of life: carpets, vessels, fine wool and silk fabrics, and jewelry.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They also owned large herds of animals, controlled the grazing lands used by them, and kept the benefits for themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Meanwhile, poverty among ordinary tribespeople became so severe that a completely destitute group known as the ṣuʿlūk emerged.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These people were forced to wander through the desert away from the settlements of their own tribes. Some survived by attacking roads, caravans, and travelers.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Poor groups like these looked toward Islam when it first appeared.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The new movement condemned monopoly, usury, and social injustice. To the poor, it seemed to offer hope that their situation might change for the better.
